summary: A 1978 list of assigned numbers used in network protocols. It replaced RFC 739 and was replaced by RFC 755. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This was a big list of which number meant which thing in the network's rules. It was later replaced by a newer list.

questions: how do protocols get numbers assigned
subtitle: A comprehensive registry of all numbers assigned in early network protocols

tldr.problem: As the ARPANET grew, many protocols needed assigned numbers (link IDs, socket numbers, network addresses). These had been scattered across different RFCs, making it hard to find current assignments.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel compiled all assigned numbers into one reference: link numbers (0–255), socket numbers (0–255), network numbers (0–255), IP versions, and protocol formats. The RFC explained each registry and managed further assignments.
tldr.outcome: This became the authoritative registry, updated periodically as new protocols and numbers were assigned. It was replaced by RFC 755, which added updates to the network numbers.

today: RFC 750 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 755. The concept of centralized number registries evolved into IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority), which maintains similar registries for the modern internet.

sections.title: The Assigned Numbers Registry
sections.content:
RFC 750 documents assigned numbers used across ARPANET protocols. Jon Postel at USC-ISI maintained the registry and allocated new numbers as protocols evolved. The RFC lists five key registries: link numbers (for the Host/IMP interface), socket numbers (for AHHP logical connections), network numbers (for the internetwork layer), IP version numbers, and protocol format identifiers.

The RFC explains that assignments are handled by Jon Postel at USC-ISI, and anyone developing a protocol needing numbers should contact him. It references the Protocol Handbook prepared by the Network Information Center for detailed specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: One person at USC kept track of all the numbers. If you made a new protocol, you'd ask Jon for some numbers to use, and he'd add them to this list.

sections.title: The Five Registries
sections.content:
Link numbers (0–255) identify which protocol runs on a Host/IMP interface. Socket numbers (0–255) are divided into ranges: 0–63 for network-wide standard functions (Telnet, FTP, Echo, Discard, etc.), 64–127 for host-specific functions, 128–223 reserved for future use, and 224–255 experimental. Network numbers (0–255) identify internetwork addresses; in 1978, 22 were assigned, including the ARPANET (10), SATNET (4), and early packet radio networks.

Internet protocol versions (0–15) identified different versions of the internet protocol then under development. Protocol format identifiers (0–255) distinguished protocols running over the internet, including raw internet, TCP variants, gateway monitoring, and others.
sections.plainLanguage: Different parts of the protocol stack needed different numbers. One set for connections, one for different networks, one for protocol versions, one for which protocol to use next.

sections.title: Governance and Updates
sections.content:
RFC 750 would be updated periodically, and current information was always available from Jon Postel. The RFC references the Protocol Handbook and the RFC series for complete specifications of listed protocols. This version obsoletes five earlier RFCs (739, 604, 503, 433, 349), consolidating scattered assignments into one authoritative source.

RFC 750 is Historic and was replaced by RFC 755 (May 1979), which added updates to network numbers and protocol assignments as the early internet continued to evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: This became the official list. When new protocols were added or new assignments made, the list was updated. Eventually a newer version replaced it.

references.text: BBN Report 1822, "The ARPANET Host-to-Host Protocol", Bolt Beranek and Newman.
